16.1. The actual contour integral and triangle theorem

Let be open. Holomorphic means complex differentiable at every point of ; continuity of the derivative is not assumed. A contour is a finite concatenation of continuously differentiable maps . Its integral is the original oriented Riemann integral

This is defined for continuous . The real and imaginary coordinate integrals, their triangle inequality and the limit of Riemann sums prove the bound. Reversing the original parameter endpoints reverses the sign. Concatenation adds the integrals, including their endpoints. A continuously differentiable increasing reparameterization retains its derivative factor by substitution; reversing the orientation changes its sign. These assertions apply to each piece separately. A zero-length piece contributes zero.

For an oriented triangle whose closed interior lies in , let . Join the side midpoints, forming four triangles with the inherited positive orientation. Each interior edge occurs twice with opposite orientation, so is the sum of their four boundary integrals. Choose a child whose integral has modulus at least , then repeat. At each step choose the first child in a fixed finite ordering satisfying that inequality; no additional infinite-choice assumption is needed. The resulting closed triangles are nested, with diameter and perimeter , where are the original diameter and perimeter. Compactness gives a common point , and the shrinking diameter makes it unique.

The boundary integrals of the first two terms are zero: the fundamental theorem on each side evaluates the respective primitives and , and the endpoint values cancel. Therefore CX1 gives

Thus every such triangle integral is zero. A degenerate triangle has zero integral directly by cancellation of its collinear oriented sides. No real partial derivative or continuity of has been used.

There is a point-removal version needed below. Suppose is continuous on a disk and holomorphic except possibly at one point . Its triangle integrals are still zero. For a triangle having as a vertex, remove the homothetic small triangle of ratio at that vertex. The remaining quadrilateral splits into two triangles avoiding , whose integrals vanish by CX3. Interior-edge cancellation makes the original integral equal the small triangle integral. On its compact neighborhood is bounded, so CX1 bounds this by , tending to zero. If is inside a triangle, split it into the three triangles joining to its vertices. If it is on an edge, split into the two triangles with as a vertex. Opposite internal sides cancel in both cases. If is outside, CX3 already applies.

For any continuous with zero triangle integrals on a disk centered at , define on that disk. The triangle with vertices gives

Continuity makes the quotient tend to . The complex derivative is also the real coordinate derivative, since the remainder is . Along every contour piece the already proved real chain rule gives . Consequently every closed contour in this disk has integral zero. This applies to the point-removal function as well; it does not assume in advance that the derivative of a holomorphic function is holomorphic.

Joint measurability on the product of its circles follows by induction on their number. For one circle it is CMI1. For , replace only the first circle parameter by its finite dyadic endpoints. As its mesh tends to zero, separate continuity in that first coordinate gives pointwise convergence to the original function for every remaining parameter tuple and every . The completed null-cylinder argument proves the claim, with the entire original tuple retained. There is no assumption that separate continuity already gives joint continuity.

Apply the original one-variable Cauchy formula successively for the fixed other coordinates. The absolute completed Fubini bound on the circle product is It comes from the full product of the differentials , not a unit circle substitute. The resulting original multiple formula is All factors have their original positive orientations; Fubini justifies reversing the iterated order as well. Differentiation of this joint series and the full coefficient integrals give Mixed derivatives of the integrand itself are supplied by the same multiple circle representation before integration in . 16.6. Bounded and exhausted maximum principles in the original domains

Suppose has a local maximum at an interior point . If , it vanishes on that neighborhood. Otherwise, if the local power series is nonconstant, let be its first nonconstant coefficient. Choose a complex unit so that is a positive real multiple of ; existence follows from the actual circle parameter by dividing that argument by the integer . For small positive , . Its component in the direction of is strictly greater than , contradicting the maximum. Thus is constant locally, and CX7's identity theorem makes it constant on the connected component. This proves the interior maximum-modulus principle.

If is bounded, is holomorphic in it and continuous on its closure, compactness gives a maximum on that closure. If it is attained in the interior, the preceding argument makes constant on that component. That bounded open component has a boundary point: follow a ray from one of its points until the first exit from a containing bounded ball and take the first component-exit limit. Its boundary lies in , because any interior ball meeting the component at a limit point would be connected to it and hence belong to the same component. Continuity therefore makes the constant value a boundary value. Consequently

The reverse inequality is immediate. Disconnected bounded domains cause no exception, since the argument applies to the component where the attained maximum lies.

Proof for an interior point. Translate to zero. Write the positive distances to the left, right, bottom and top sides as , respectively. The translated rectangle is . For each angle , take the applicable positive numbers in the following list: Let be their minimum. At least one number is applicable. The inequalities defining the rectangle say exactly that its intersection with this ray is the segment of radii . Thus is its unique boundary point on the ray.

The active side changes only at the four corner directions. On an interval between corner directions, the relevant displayed quotient is smooth with a nonzero denominator. Near an axis, a quotient with denominator tending to zero cannot be the minimum because the other applicable quotient stays bounded. At a corner the two active quotients have the same positive value. These facts prove that is positive, continuous, -periodic and piecewise . They also give a finite partition on which its parametrization is smooth.

As increases by , these boundary points traverse each of the four sides once in positive order.
